results.title: Gendered Access to Formal and Informal Resources in Postdisaster Development in the Ecuadorian Andes
results.content: We present a methodology that is replicable in a wide variety of disaster, resettlement, and development settings, and we advocate an inductive, evidence-based approach to policy, built upon an understanding of local gender, class, and ethnic dynamics affecting access to formal and informal resources. Gender-based inequalities contribute to vulnerability in disasters and resettlement in many ways, affecting division of labor, access to formal and informal resources, and transmission of information through gendered social networks. However, studies of informal social support exchanges in disaster contexts tend to find that men give and receive more support outside their kin networks than do women (Drabek 1986; Hurlbert et al 2001). In a study of social support exchanges among nonrelatives in the postdisaster resettlement community of Penipe Nuevo, Ecuador (one of the sites of this study), Burke (2010) found that men both gave and received more social support than women. Informational support exchanges only varied significantly by gender in Penipe Nuevo (Table 3), where men were again more likely than women to receive information. Informational support exchanges only exhibited significant variation by gender in the relocation site of Penipe Nuevo, where both men and women were more likely to provide informational support to men than to women. This study identified important gendered dynamics affecting access to formal and informal support in disaster-affected communities and new settlements in highland Ecuador. * In other communities, men give and receive more of a specific kind of support, such as in landed new settlements where men develop new relations of reciprocity (Pusuca), and in fragmented agricultural communities that predate the disaster that rely on male–male relations for distribution of resources (San Juan). * Other communities show few differences by gender in access to support, such as highly organized or socially cohesive agricultural communities that predate the disaster (Pillate), and long-established urban communities where women might predictably employ men for various kinds of labor (Penipe Viejo). In general, our findings call for targeted strategies to promote increased access to formal support for women and female-headed households, and for development strategies that avoid either reifying gendered hierarchies or disrupting existing informal exchange practices that are critical to survival.

results.title: How Women and Men Experience the City. Gender in an Informal Urban Context - Urbanet
results.content: Gender in an Informal Urban Context. With this in mind, key aspects of informal living, including socio-political realities, economic factors and material issues are explored here in relation to gender. The purpose is to consider the particularities that living informally can produce for gendered relations. Arguably, these trends are further complicated by informal living, which shapes meanings of being female and male and patterns of gendered relationships in a myriad of ways, remembering that ultimately these are also affected by the wider political, cultural and economic processes within which informal settlements exist. In a socio-political sense, urban informal living offers some elements of freedom for women. Arguably, women can enter the informal sector more readily than the formal and this is especially true for female headed households, enhancing women’s ability to set up and ‘own’ their own house, provide shelter for children, and establish a base in the city to sleep, live and work from. Informal spaces foster potential for female leadership, as informal politics often persists in such settings and community networks can prove effective, providing significant gendered support. Well-located informal spaces can offer improved access to education, health and policing facilities, but this is highly variable and for many, the absence of formal childcare or well-located schooling frequently hampers women’s efforts to support their families. For men, informal living can symbolise failure as pressures to provide proper housing for families proves elusive. Informal living, because of its often poor material reality (non-soundproof, relatively easily broken into), does however mean that in situations of domestic violence, women’s screams will illicit beneficial responses from neighbours, affording higher communal protection than may be enjoyed in more formal, private settings. In short, informal settlements meet urgent housing needs in cities, often benefiting poor women and their families, and they will continue to be a reality of all cities in the global South in the foreseeable future. Eradicating informal settlements without providing well-located affordable alternatives has dire consequences for women and men, increasing women’s vulnerability in particular. The gendered realities that informal settlements foster need to be analysed and addressed to improve the living conditions of all inhabitants. Gender in an Informal Urban Context - 7.

results.title: Sexual Harassment and Service Labor: Strategies and Relational Practices - Farrugia - 2025 - Gender, Work & Organization - Wiley Online Library
results.content: Sexual harassment and gender-based violence are longstanding concerns in studies of service work, but are typically analyzed in terms of interactions between workers and consumers within gendered definitions of “good service,” neglecting the role of relationships amongst workers as a critical context that facilitates or constrains how workers can respond. Inspired by the insights generated through such a relational focus, this paper makes new contributions to studies of gender and service labor by exploring individual, relational and collective strategies that service workers use to respond to the threat of sexual harassment while at work, and situates informal relationships amongst workers as critical to the dynamics of sexual harassment and the gendered power relations of service labor. Aligning with Coffey et al.'s (2023) concept of femininity work, a key argument of this paper is that the practices that service workers use to respond to sexual harassment are also part of this broader terrain of gendered relational practice. Sexual harassment is one critical way that the gendered power relations of interactive service work are enacted, including the gendered dynamics of consumer sovereignty and “good service,” and the general precarity and low status that limit workers' control over the labor process and over their positioning at work. Nevertheless, in foregrounding the experiences of these workers, this paper has tried to position interactive service work as a site where women competently manage and deliberately contest the gendered and sexualized power relationships of the service labor process and the gendered relations of precarious work. One of the key findings of this paper is that sexual harassment is contingent on the local social relations of specific venues, and on the disciplinary requirements of work in different service industries, for example, the relative autonomy that hospitality workers as opposed to call-center workers are accorded in managing service interactions autonomously. (2023) have shown that migrant workers are excluded from the informal social relationships that often provide access to service employment, and given the importance of these informal relationships for the way that workers respond to sexual harassment, this exclusion is likely to impact on migrant women's experiences of gendered and sexualized power relations at work.
